deep.reconstruction:
Setting. (α_n) is a decreasing sequence of positive numbers, not all zero. Two exponents are defined:
- ρ = inf{s>0 : α_n = O(n^{-1/s})}, with ρ = +∞ if no such s exists.
- σ = inf{s>0 : Σ α_n^s < ∞}. This is the classical exponent of convergence.

Claim. ρ = σ, and 1/ρ can be expressed by a lim sup/lim inf of log(1/α_n)/log n.

σ ≤ ρ is immediate. If α_n ≤ C n^{-1/s}, then Σ α_n^t converges for every t > s.

ρ ≤ σ follows from a lemma. If Σ α_n^s < ∞ and α_n is decreasing, then α_n = o(n^{-1/s}). Grothendieck first wrote 'O', crossed it out and replaced it with 'o', and notes that monotonicity is essential.

Proof of the lemma.
- Put β_n = α_n^s; this reduces to s = 1.
- Suppose α_{n_i} ≥ 1/n_i along a strictly increasing sequence n_i.
- By monotonicity, the block sum α_{n_{i-1}+1}+…+α_{n_i} ≥ (n_i − n_{i-1})/n_i =: ε_i.
- The blocks are disjoint, so Σ ε_i ≤ Σ α_n < ∞. Also ε_i < 1.
- Then n_i = n_{i-1}/(1−ε_i) = n_0/∏_{k≤i}(1−ε_k) ≤ n_0/∏_{k≥1}(1−ε_k) < ∞, since the infinite product is positive.
- So (n_i) is bounded, which contradicts strict increase. Hence α_n < 1/n eventually.
- Applying this to α_n/ε for each ε > 0 gives o(1/n).

This is Olivier's theorem (Abel–Olivier–Pringsheim) on monotone convergent series. The proof via the infinite product of the block ratios is a cute non-standard variant. The usual proof is the Cauchy-condensation-style estimate (n/2)α_n ≤ Σ_{n/2<k≤n} α_k → 0.

Purpose. On the next page Grothendieck takes Σα_i < ∞ and f(z) = ∏(1+α_i z). He shows the order of this entire function equals ρ (= σ). He does this by comparison with the model case α_n = n^{-β}, splitting the product at ν ≈ r^{1/β}, and recalls the formula for the order via the maximal term.

This is the classical Borel/Hadamard theorem: the order of a canonical product of genus 0 equals the convergence exponent of its zeros. The previous page proves that a genus-zero function decaying exponentially in a sector vanishes. In context, the material is preparation for estimating the growth of Fredholm determinants det(1+zu) of nuclear (p-summable) operators in terms of the summability exponent of their eigenvalues. That theme appears in Grothendieck's 'La théorie de Fredholm' (1956) and in Produits tensoriels topologiques (1955).
errors: The formula '1/ρ = lim sup_n log(1/α_n)/log n' should be lim inf. α_n = O(n^{-1/s}) for all n means log(1/α_n)/log n ≥ 1/s − o(1) for all large n. So the supremum of admissible 1/s is the lim inf. For decreasing step-like sequences the lim sup can be strictly larger.
In the product formula he writes n_i = 1/((1−ε_1)…(1−ε_n)). The numerator should be n_0, the first index, not 1. This is harmless for boundedness.
The lemma as finally stated (o rather than O) needs the remark that the argument applies to α_n/ε for every ε > 0. As written it only shows α_n < 1/n eventually. This is a minor gap.

ideas.what: Equality of the 'O-exponent' and the convergence exponent for decreasing sequences
ideas.modern_name: exponent of convergence / Lorentz-type equivalence ℓ^{s,∞} ⊂ ℓ^{t} for t>s for decreasing sequences
ideas.usually_credited_to: classical (Borel, Lindelöf; standard in entire-function texts)
ideas.where_published: Possibly used implicitly in Produits tensoriels topologiques / La théorie de Fredholm when discussing operators of order p

ideas.what: Monotone convergent series have terms o(1/n), proved via a product of block ratios
Order of ∏(1+α_i z) equals the convergence exponent of (α_i) (continued on the next page)
ideas.modern_name: Borel's theorem on order of canonical products
ideas.where_published: Related use in 'La théorie de Fredholm' (Bull. SMF 1956) for growth of Fredholm determinants

deep.surprise_reason: These are textbook facts from classical entire-function theory, rederived by Grothendieck as tools, presumably for Fredholm determinants of nuclear operators. The only individual touch is the non-standard product argument for Olivier's theorem, which has no research significance.
transcription_corrections: '(α_n étant diminuant[?]!)' most likely reads '(α_n étant décroissant!)', stressing monotonicity.
The interlinear addition at the top is hard to read. It may be 'et non presque tous nuls' or similar rather than 'et non partout nulle'; it is uncertain.
The partly illegible line after the lim sup formula plausibly says that 1/ρ is written as a bound for a set, from which one easily deduces σ ≤ ρ.
The product denominator should be read with n_0 (the starting index) in the numerator; 'ε_n' at the end should be 'ε_i'.
